listing_view.reasoning: Subscription hit ~87x with the steepest jump on the final day (from ~12x to ~87x), which is classic QIB/last-day behaviour that historically supports a strong debut. Priced at ~15x latest basic EPS against a stated industry average of 113x [verified figures], the pricing leaves clear headroom for a pop regardless of whether that benchmark is meaningful. The cap on my score is that grey-market premium, anchor book and the composition of the demand are all unknown, and the fresh-issue-vs-offer-size contradiction means I cannot even confirm the deal structure.

longterm_view.reasoning: Growth (revenue +19.7% latest year, PAT compounding ~34%) and a 24% ROCE look good, but this is a Mumbai-region redevelopment developer [business, page 226] whose profits are not converting to cash — operating cash flow was -₹412m and -₹926m in the two latest years against PAT of ₹713m and ₹623m. Leverage above 1x equity with lender-imposed restrictive covenants [business, page 358], thin liquidity (current ratio 1.16), and dependence on a limited number of contractors and suppliers [business, page 386] make the equity story fragile even if reported returns stay high. Falling ROE/ROCE as the book scales is the usual signature of cash being absorbed faster than profit is earned.

governance.reasoning: No promoter shares are pledged or encumbered as of the RHP date [capital_structure, page 84], which is genuinely positive, though the document contemplates future pledging for loans [capital_structure, page 85]. Beyond that the extracts contain only boilerplate materiality policies [litigation, page 391], so the evidence base for judging governance is thin rather than reassuring.

key_risks.risk: Profits are not turning into cash
key_risks.why_it_matters: Operating cash flow was negative in two of three years (-₹926m, -₹412m) while PAT grew, meaning earnings exist on paper while the business consumes cash; a developer that never self-funds must keep borrowing or diluting.

Debt-to-equity ~1.1 with debt nearly tripling in two years, and lenders have imposed restrictive covenants, so a project delay or market slowdown can quickly become a solvency issue rather than a margin issue.

Operations are concentrated in the highly competitive MCGM region with dependence on a limited number of contractors and suppliers, so a local demand downturn or a single contractor failure hits the whole P&L.
The fresh-issue figure exceeds the total offer size in the data, so the split between money going to the company versus sellers is unknown — a material gap when judging who the listing is priced for.

answers.question: is the peer set fairly chosen, and are the peers themselves expensive rather than this being cheap?
answers.answer: Not assessable as framed, but treat the 113x benchmark with deep suspicion. Zero peer rows were parsed from the document, so I cannot check who is in the average; a 113x industry P/E for Indian real estate is so far above plausible sector norms that it almost certainly reflects a cherry-picked or distorted peer set (tiny-loss makers or one-off inflated multiples) rather than a fair cohort. The 15x offer multiple is therefore 'cheap versus a number I do not trust' — it may still be sensibly priced, but the prospectus's own comparison cannot be used to prove it.

answers.question: where did the money go — receivables, inventory, or both?
answers.answer: Predominantly inventory/project work-in-progress, not receivables. Receivable days actually improved from 61 to 30 over three years, so customers are paying faster; yet operating cash flow was -₹926m then -₹412m while revenue grew 42% and 20%. The only consistent explanation is cash being sunk into construction spend and land/redevelopment project assets — the stated dependence on contractors and suppliers for project execution [business, page 386] and the redevelopment model [business, page 226]. The extracts do not give a working-capital breakdown, so I cannot separate inventory from advances to contractors with certainty.

answer.what_would_change_my_mind: A cash-flow note or working-capital schedule showing the negative operating cash flow is timing-driven with projects nearing completion and sales bookings converting would materially lift the long-term view; conversely, evidence the offer is heavily weighted to an offer-for-sale, or a credible peer set confirming the 113x benchmark is fabricated, would push me lower.
